Title: March 26, 2026 - Boulder City Council Study Session (joint with Planning Board)
Overview: Boulder Valley School District presented declining enrollment, with about 3,600 fewer students since 2017 and a projected further drop of about 1,700, and outlined community engagement sessions in April with possible school consolidation decisions in fall 2026. Council then met with the Planning Board to review the draft Boulder Valley Comprehensive Plan, with consensus on strong support for housing diversity, 15-minute neighborhoods, and the simplified land use framework, while a straw poll on expanding neighborhood-two designations along transit corridors did not reach consensus. No formal votes were taken; refinements return at the April 13 four-body meeting, with public comments due April 6 and adoption hearings planned for June.

Topic1.Title: BVSD Declining Enrollment Update
Topic1.Summary: Boulder Valley School District leaders presented enrollment data showing a sustained decline of more than 3,600 students since 2017, with about 525 lost this year alone and a projected further drop of about 1,700 students. Elementary schools are most affected, with roughly 4,800 open seats district-wide and many Boulder schools falling below two classes per grade level. The district outlined community engagement sessions in April, staff option development over the summer, and a final plan for board action in October, with potential consolidations or closures and a stated goal of reinvesting savings in classrooms. Council members asked about long-term projections, the city role in reusing surplus buildings, and how the city can get involved early in neighborhood-level changes.

Topic2.Title: Comprehensive Plan Overview by Staff
Topic2.Summary: Staff presented the draft Boulder Valley Comprehensive Plan, reorganized into six chapters with a new implementation chapter and glossary, and reduced the policy list from 210 to 102. The update was shaped by 69 engagement opportunities, community assembly recommendations, and 23 community change requests moved into the draft. The draft simplifies the future land use map into four classes and 12 designations, shifting from parcel-by-parcel mapping to neighborhood-scale planning. Staff projected about a 35 percent increase in housing capacity, more balanced housing types, and about 11 percent more job capacity, while noting these are modeled estimates rather than forecasts.

Topic3.Title: Council Clarifying Questions on the Draft Plan
Topic3.Summary: Council asked why some policies, such as those on the municipal airport and specific financing tools, are more operational than others, and staff said the goal is to keep the plan visionary with examples rather than fixed rules. Questions covered how the plan addresses wildfire fuels mitigation, whether zoning will conflict with new land use designations, and how the strategic plan and department plans will be approved, with the answer that council will vote on the citywide strategic plan. Members also asked about student versus non-student population growth, community hub capacity, the mismatch between transportation and land use, and how the plan connects to the 2023 community survey.

Topic4.Title: Consensus on Alignment and Strongly Supported Elements
Topic4.Summary: Members broadly agreed the draft reflects community feedback, praising the depth of engagement and the community assembly contributions. Strong support was expressed for the expanded housing types in neighborhood one and two areas, the 15-minute neighborhood concept, the integration of land use and transportation, and new policies on social infrastructure, natural infrastructure, and the night and visitor economy. Several members also praised the equity-focused first policy and the simplified land use designations, while one member stressed the need for stronger acknowledgment of tribal treaties and land back.

Topic5.Title: Refinements, Neighborhood Character, and Transit Corridor Designations
Topic5.Summary: Members suggested refinements including clearer transportation and Vision Zero language, stronger wildfire and fuels mitigation in open space policies, better emergency communication language, clearer service level agreement processes for water, and a glossary definition for neighborhood character. Discussion of policy 24 on neighborhood character was contentious, with some arguing the term is exclusionary and others defending it as describing neighborhood personality. Planning Board members and council split on a straw poll to have staff study expanding neighborhood-two designations beyond transit corridors, with no consensus reached. Staff agreed to report back with proposed revisions and flagged items needing city-county discussion on April 13.

Topic6.Title: Next Steps and Adoption Timeline
Topic6.Summary: Staff asked members to send written feedback to the project email by April 6, the close of the public comment period, and noted that all comments will be logged with rationale and shared with the recommended plan. A four-body meeting with the county commissioners and planning commission is set for April 13 to resolve lingering issues. The recommended plan will be released May 18, with a joint public hearing on June 4. Staff confirmed that the plan becomes effective upon final approval by all four bodies.
